verses.translation_literal: A psalm of David. YHWH, hear my prayer, give ear to my supplications; in your faithfulness answer me, in your righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of David. O LORD, hear me. Hear my prayer; bend down your ear to my pleading. Answer me by your faithfulness, answer me by your righteousness.
verses.directors_commentary:
The man speaking is not asking for what he has earned. Notice the two things he invokes: God's faithfulness and God's righteousness. Both are the Lord's own qualities, not his. Play the opening as an appeal to a promise already made, not a bargain. Rashi hears 'faithfulness' as the promise God gave; Radak, too, reads it as 'your word is true'.

The KJV smooths the final clause with an 'and' ("and in thy righteousness") that Hebrew does not have: the line simply trails off, 'in your righteousness', as if he cannot finish. Meiri notes the missing 'and' and reads it as 'in your faithfulness and in your righteousness'. The prayer opens with three near-synonyms for being heard (hear, give ear, answer), a pile-up of verbs that tells you how desperate he is. The note that the heading ('A psalm of David') is verse 1 in the Hebrew but verse 0 in the KJV does not change the sense.

philological_notes.note: 'My pleas for favour'. It comes from the root of grace, חן: a supplication is a request for an undeserved gift, not a claim. Malbim distinguishes 'prayer' (the fixed, general petitions) from 'supplications' (the individual's particular needs).
'In your faithfulness', literally what makes something firm and reliable. Rashi glosses it as God's keeping the promise he made.

verses.translation_literal: And do not come in judgment with your servant, for no living [one] is righteous before you.
verses.translation_dramatic: But do not bring your servant to trial. Do not set me before your bench. For who among the living could stand up straight before you and be found in the right?
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm, and the speaker's courage is in what he refuses to claim. He has just invoked God's righteousness (v. 1); now he begs not to be judged by it. 'Come in judgment' is a legal phrase: to enter a courtroom case. In the ancient world a petitioner who 'is righteous' (yitsdaq) is the one the court declares in the right. He says that no one alive can win that verdict against God. 'Servant' is also a legal word: a client of a great lord, who asks for the lord's loyalty, not his inspection.

The KJV's 'in thy sight shall no man living be justified' makes a theological abstraction ('justified') and inserts 'man'; the Hebrew says kol chai, 'anything alive', 'any living [one]'. It is wider and plainer. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as: if I have sinned, do not punish me now, in my distress, for who could stand if you checked every deed? Metzudat David reads it as a plea to be treated by mercy, not by repayment.

philological_notes.note: אֶת here is the preposition 'with', as in 'enter into judgment with'; it is not the object marker. Ibn Ezra says it is the same as עם.

'Be in the right' (a court term: be declared innocent). It is the same root as 'righteousness' (צִדְקָה) in verse 1, so the psalm turns on a single word: God's righteousness is the speaker's hope in v. 1 and the standard none can meet in v. 2.

verses.translation_literal: For an enemy has pursued my soul, has crushed to the ground my life; he has made me sit in dark places like the dead of long ago.
verses.translation_dramatic: For an enemy has run my soul to ground. He has ground my life into the dust. He has set me down in the dark places, among the dead of long ago.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the danger is named, and it is physical. The verbs run downward in three steps: pursue, crush, seat. 'Pursued' is the hunter's verb, and 'crushed to the ground' is what a hunter's quarry or a trampled man becomes. The word for 'my life' (chayyati) is a poetic noun from the root of 'live'; Metzudat Zion equates it with the nefesh, the living self, so what is flattened is the very life in him.

The last image is the sharpest. 'He has made me sit' (hoshivani) is the verb that normally gives a person a seat of honour; here it seats him in 'dark places' (machashakkim), the place of the dead, among 'the dead of long ago' (metei olam). The KJV's 'as those that have been long dead' is accurate, but its 'smitten' for 'crushed' loses the powdering sense of the Hebrew. Radak, following the superscription tradition, pictures David hiding in the back of the cave in Saul's pursuit, as good as dead in the dark. Rashi reads the whole psalm as Israel in exile. Direct it as a man for whom the grave has already begun.

philological_notes.note: 'Crushed, pulverised'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as breaking into pieces. Ibn Ezra hears in it contempt and disgrace.
'Dark places', a plural of place used for Sheol-like darkness (Lam 3:6 has the same phrase for the dead). Radak reads it as the back of the cave.
'The dead of antiquity', those long dead, with no one left to remember them. Radak says that people give up hope for these more than for the recently dead.

verses.translation_literal: And my spirit wraps itself over me; within me my heart is appalled.
verses.translation_dramatic: My spirit folds itself over me like a shroud. And in my chest my heart stands stunned, emptied, struck dumb.
verses.directors_commentary:
The outer darkness (v. 3) now enters the body. The verb titattef, 'wraps itself', is the image of a cloak thrown over the head, or of a faint: the spirit has covered itself over the speaker as if to hide. The same verb is used in the previous psalm group for fainting (Ps 142:4). Ibn Ezra reads it as the mind folding in on itself, thought upon thought. 'Wrap' as the image of a garment makes it grim: he is dressed in his own collapse.

The second half doubles the first, which is typical of Hebrew parallelism: 'within me' (betokhi) repeats what 'over me' says, from the inside. Yishtomem, 'is appalled', is the verb of stunned silence; Rashi cites Ezekiel 3:15, where the prophet sat seven days 'stunned' among the exiles, and Tamar 'desolate' in 2 Samuel 13:20. The KJV's 'desolate' is the same word in its other sense, 'laid waste'. Both are meant: stunned and emptied. The Targum reads it more gently, as the heart growing sluggish.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael of עטף: 'wrap oneself, be faint'. It has both the clothing sense and the swooning sense; the speaker's own spirit is the garment.
'Be stunned, be desolate': dumb astonishment and emptiness at once. Rashi ties it to a word for dullness and amazement.

verses.translation_literal: I have remembered days from of old; I have meditated on all your doing; on the work of your hands I muse.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have gone back. I have gone back to the days of old, and I have turned over everything you did, slowly, the way one turns a stone in the palm. And now, in the dark, I speak softly to myself of the work of your hands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The man has been crushed to silence in verse 4, and here he does the one thing left to him: he looks backward. Play the verse as a slow, deliberate act, not as nostalgia. In the ancient Near East a petitioner argued his case by recalling what the god had already done, and Israel's prayers do this constantly: the past deeds of the LORD are the collateral for a present request. The verse is built as a staircase of three verbs, remembering, meditating, musing, and the object grows more concrete each time: 'days', then 'all your doing', then 'the work of your hands'.

The KJV puts all three verbs in the present ('I remember … I meditate … I muse'). The Hebrew has two perfects ('I have remembered', 'I have meditated') and a closing imperfect ('I muse'): the first two read as things already done, the last as what he is doing now. The KJV also gives 'thy works' for po'al, which is better rendered as the doing itself, the activity, and then 'work of thy hands' for ma'aseh, the finished thing. Malbim draws that very distinction: ma'aseh is the finished product and po'al the engagement in it. The two verbs hagah and siaḥ are both audible words: hagah is a low murmur, as of a dove or a man reading aloud to himself, and siaḥ is talking things over. Ancient meditation was never silent; let the actor mutter.

philological_notes.note: To murmur, mutter, ponder aloud. The same root gives hegyon in Ps 19:15 (the meditation of my heart), which Metzudat Zion cites. Meditation here is a voiced, repeated act, not a silent thought.

From siaḥ, to speak, complain, converse. Ibn Ezra notes that it is a verb whose middle letter is weak and whose last letter is doubled. Metzudat Zion glosses it as speech. The vowel pattern is a poel-type form, 'I keep musing'.

verses.translation_literal: I have spread out my hands to you; my soul [is] like an exhausted land to you. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: I spread out my hands to you, palms open, empty. My soul is a parched and weary land, and it lies open to you. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The gesture is physical: the hands spread out and up, palms open, the posture of prayer in the ancient Near East (compare 1 Kings 8:22, Solomon's hands 'spread toward heaven'). Ibn Ezra's reason is practical: a beggar holds out his hands for what will be put into them. The man who was 'pulverised' now offers empty hands.

The simile 'like an exhausted land' needs the climate: this is a country of dry riverbeds, where the earth in summer cracks and waits for the first rain. The KJV adds the verb 'thirsteth', which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew has only 'my soul like a weary land to you', with the verb left out, so the longing is carried by the picture alone. Metzudat Zion notes that 'ayefah', 'weary', is a borrowed word: the weary one is thirsty, so the land is described as the thirsty one. Rashi reads the dry land as the exile. 'Selah' is a liturgical marker whose meaning we do not know; it probably marks a pause or a lift in the music.

philological_notes.note: 'Faint, exhausted'; of land, 'parched'. Metzudat Zion explains that weariness is thirst, and the word is used of land by extension.
A liturgical or musical term of uncertain meaning, probably a pause or a rise; it is left untranslated.

verses.translation_literal: Hurry, answer me, YHWH; my spirit is spent. Do not hide your face from me, or I will be made equal with those going down [to] the pit.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hurry, LORD, and answer me. My spirit is spent. Do not hide your face from me, or I will be counted among those who go down to the pit.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prayer has been patient; now it breaks into a short, urgent line. 'Hurry' (maher) is an imperative, with no 'speedily' softening: it is the shout of a man who has no time. 'My spirit is spent' uses the verb of finishing, kalah: it has come to its end, as eyes 'fail' with longing in Deuteronomy 28:65, as Rashi notes. Radak: I am almost dead.

The fear is the hidden face. In the ancient Near East to see the king's face was to be received by him; to have it hidden was to be dismissed or abandoned. The 'pit' (bor) is the word for the grave and for the underworld, where the dead are cut off from God; to 'go down' is the standard movement into it. The KJV's 'lest I be like unto them' is correct in sense, but the Hebrew has 'and I will be made equal (nimshalti) with', a verb of comparison and ranking: counted as one of them, a number in the roll of the dead. Meiri allows that 'those who go down to the pit' can mean the wicked as well as the dead.

philological_notes.note: 'Is finished, spent'. The verb of ending; Rashi relates it to the failing of the eyes and spirit from longing without reaching what is desired.
'Pit, cistern': the grave and the realm of the dead. Meiri reads it as the grave or, in a figurative sense, the wicked.

token_glosses.gloss: and I will be made like

verses.translation_literal: Make me hear in the morning your covenant loyalty, for in you I have trusted; make me know the way which I shall walk, for to you I have lifted up my soul.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the morning bring me your word, and let it be your faithful love that I hear. I have put my trust in you, and in nothing else. Show me the road that I must walk, for to you, only to you, I have lifted my whole self.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the night of verses 3 to 7, the speaker asks for morning, and what he wants from it is a sound: 'make me hear'. Chesed is not 'lovingkindness' in the KJV's coinage, a sweetness; it is covenant loyalty, the LORD keeping the bond he swore, and the man is asking to hear that spoken as a verdict. Morning matters because ancient courts and rescues alike came with first light, and the Psalms often picture the LORD's help arriving at dawn. Radak reads night as the time of trouble and morning as the time of deliverance, and Ibn Ezra notes that most journeys and tasks begin in the morning.

The second request is for direction: 'make me know the way'. The word zu here is the poetic relative 'which', so the line asks to be shown the road he must take; Metzudat David glosses it as 'the way which I shall walk' (הדרך אשר אלך בה). The KJV's 'wherein I should walk' is a fair rendering of that sense, though it adds a 'should' that the Hebrew imperfect leaves open. Both requests stand on a 'for': he trusts, and he has lifted his nefesh. The KJV's 'soul' is right as far as it goes, but nefesh is also the throat, the appetite, the whole needy self, and lifting it is the gesture of one who holds up an empty vessel. Ibn Ezra and Meiri compare Deut 24:15, where the poor man 'lifts his nefesh' to his wage, that is, stakes his life on it.

philological_notes.note: A poetic relative particle, 'which, that', as in 'the way which I shall walk'. Not a demonstrative 'this'. STEPBible also glosses it 'which', and Metzudat David paraphrases the phrase as 'the way in which I shall walk'.

'I have lifted up my soul': an idiom for directing one's longing and trust to someone. Ibn Ezra and Meiri cite 'and he lifts up his soul to it' (Deut 24:15) as the sense of hope; Meiri adds the sense of prayer, as in Lam 3:41.
Covenant loyalty: faithful love that holds to a pledge. Not mere kindness. Heard 'in the morning', it is the answer of a God who keeps his bond.

verses.translation_literal: Deliver me from my enemies, YHWH; to you I have covered.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rescue me from my enemies, LORD. I have come to you to be hidden.
verses.directors_commentary:
A short, hard line with a famous problem. The first half is plain: 'deliver me' is the verb of snatching a person out of danger, said to the Lord as to a champion. The second half, el'eikha kissiti, is literally 'to you I have covered'. It has no object, and no one agrees on what is covered. The KJV's 'I flee unto thee to hide me' quietly rewrites it, treating kissiti as if it were chasiti, 'I have taken refuge' (the verb of Psalm 7:1, 'in you I take refuge'); the English versions follow it, and the Hebrew does not say it.

The older Jewish commentators take the plain verb: I have covered. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David say that he has hidden his troubles from everyone else and told them to God alone, since human help is worthless; Ibn Ezra and Malbim similarly. Meiri reads 'deliver me' as a noun-like infinitive ('my rescue from my enemies is for you'), and hears 'for your sake I hid it from all'. The Targum reads 'I have made your word my redeemer'. Direct it as a man who has told nobody; the prayer is the first time he speaks.

philological_notes.note: 'I have covered' (Piel perfect of כסה). The object is not stated. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David read 'I have hidden my troubles from others and told them to you'; the KJV reads as if from חסה 'take refuge'. Ibn Ezra rejects the identification with חסה on grammatical grounds.

verses.translation_literal: Teach me to do your will, for you [are] my God; your spirit [is] good; may it lead me in a land of level ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: Teach me to do what you want, for you are my God. Your spirit is good. Let it lead me over level ground, where no foot stumbles.
verses.directors_commentary:
After rescue, instruction. The petitioner asks for more than safety; he asks to be taught to do God's will. The reason he gives is not a debt but a relationship: 'for you are my God'. A servant (see v. 2, v. 12) asks his master to teach the household's way of doing things.

'Your spirit is good' stands alone in the Hebrew, with no 'let': it is a statement, as the accents mark it, and the English 'let your good Spirit' (BBE) makes it a wish. The Targum reads 'your holy spirit', which Malbim follows (the Holy Spirit); Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion read ruach as 'will' or 'power', that is God's good disposition. The KJV's 'land of uprightness' hides the geography: eretz mishor is 'a land of level ground', a plain with no rocks to trip on, the opposite of the broken ground and cave in which he has been hiding. Radak: 'a straight way in which I will not stumble'. 'Uprightness' is the ethical sense; the Hebrew gives the road first.

philological_notes.note: 'Your spirit is good'. Read variously as God's good will (Radak, Metzudat Zion citing Isaiah 37:7 for 'spirit' as 'will'), or God's holy spirit (Targum, Malbim).
'Level ground, a plain', and by extension 'uprightness'. Radak explains it as a straight road with no stumbling.

verses.translation_literal: For the sake of your name, YHWH, you will keep me alive; in your righteousness you will bring my soul out of trouble.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the sake of your name, LORD, keep me alive. In your righteousness, bring my soul out of its narrow place.
verses.directors_commentary:
The ground of the whole appeal is given: not his merit, but God's name. In the ancient world a god's name was his reputation, and a god who let his own servant die would be mocked by the nations (compare Exodus 32:12). Radak and Metzudat David both read 'for your name's sake' as: so that your name will be great among people when you rescue me.

The KJV's 'quicken me' is old English for 'make alive', and the verb itself is the same as in Ezekiel 37, 'cause to live'. 'Righteousness' returns from verse 1, now clearly meaning God's saving justice, which acts for the right party, not a court's verdict (v. 2). The verbs are imperfects, not commands: 'you will keep me alive' is the form of confident hope, and the English versions turn it into an imperative to match the context. 'Out of trouble': tsarah is from the root 'to be narrow, tight', so the Hebrew image is being brought out of a tight place, which continues the cave and the pit.

philological_notes.note: 'From trouble'; the noun comes from the root 'be narrow', so the picture is a tight place. The same root gives 'my adversaries' (צֹרְרֵי) in the next verse.
'For the sake of your name': so that your reputation is upheld. Radak and Metzudat David read it as 'so that your name will be magnified and sanctified'.

verses.translation_literal: And in your covenant loyalty you will destroy my enemies, and you will make perish all the adversaries of my soul, for I [am] your servant.
verses.translation_dramatic: And in your steadfast love, silence my enemies. Wipe out every one who closes in on my soul. For I am your servant.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends where it began, with a servant. 'I am your servant' (ani avdekha) closes the circle opened by 'your servant' in verse 2: he would not be judged as a servant, and now he claims the servant's right. A lord in the ancient Near East owed protection to those who served him; a lord who let his servant be destroyed lost face. Metzudat David says it plainly: it is for the master to rescue his servant from those who rise against him.

The verbs are strong. Tatsmit, 'you will cut off', is the verb of silencing and annihilation (Psalm 54:7: 'cut them off in your truth'); Metzudat Zion links it to that verse. The KJV's 'afflict my soul' for tsorerei nafshi softens it: tsorer is 'the one who binds, tightens, besieges', from the same root as 'trouble' (tsarah) in verse 11. The enemies are those who make him narrow. Note, too, that the enemy is destroyed 'in your hesed', the loyalty that was invoked in verse 8; for the psalmist, loyalty to a servant means force against his enemies. Radak: 'because I am your servant and they are not'.

philological_notes.note: 'You will cut off, silence, annihilate'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'cut off', and cites Psalm 54:7.
'The adversaries of my life': the participle of צרר, 'bind, press, besiege', which shares its root with 'trouble' (צָרָה) in v. 11.
